title: Manchester to host world leaders at G20 summit in 2027
description: World leaders, including Donald Trump, will head to Manchester next year for the G20 leaders' summit.Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is the former ma
body: World leaders, including Donald Trump, will head to Manchester next year for the G20 leaders' summit.Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is the former mayor of Greater Manchester, said he was "really pleased" he would be welcoming the US president to the city.The G20 summit, an annual gathering of the world's biggest economies, will take place on 27 and 28 November 2027 at the Manchester Central Convention Centre.  It will be the largest summit ever held in the city.Manchester was chosen earlier this year, prior to Burnham becoming prime minister. Downing Street said preparations will now step up, with hundreds of local people expected to be involved.In June, as it looked likely Burnham would become prime minister, Trump called him "the mayor of a town".Burnham told reporters that in the first phone call between the pair, he told the president: "Manchester isn't 'some town'…this is Manchester". He said the "right thing to do" was to laugh about it and "move beyond it".When he was mayor, Burnham told the Manchester Evening News, external that he "wouldn't welcome" a visit from the American president.But on his way to New York, where he will meet Trump for the first time on Tuesday, he said "politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in".Speaking to the BBC, Councillor Garry Bridges, the new leader of Manchester City Council, said an event like this would have been "unthinkable a couple of years ago" and that he hoped it would change Trump's perception of Manchester.The UK has hosted the G20 before, in 2009 in London. The cost of the security operation at the time was estimated at £7.2m.As well as the summit in Manchester, there will be events across the country next year as the UK takes on the G20 presidency. The presidency is currently held by the United States, with this year's summit taking place in Miami in December.The G20 brings together 19 of the world's largest economies, plus representatives from the European Union and the African Union. It represents about two-thirds of the world's entire population and more than 85% of the world's wealth. The annual event was first set up in 1999 with the aim of promoting financial stability and cooperation.

schema.headline: Manchester to host world leaders at G20 summit in 2027

title: Paramount reaches settlement with states in $110bn Warner Bros merger
description: Paramount Skydance has settled a lawsuit with a dozen US states, paving the way for its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. Under the
body: Paramount Skydance has settled a lawsuit with a dozen US states, paving the way for its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. Under the agreement, Paramount must produce at least 30 films a year and ensure a certain percentage are produced in the US, or face penalties including selling off parts of its business.The deal clears one of the final hurdles for the merger that is set to reshape Hollywood, combining legacy studios, major streamers, and national networks under one umbrella. Announcing the settlement, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the agreement was "not a vote of support for this merger", while Parmount's chief executive welcomed the resolution.David Ellison said that now the state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America (WGA) concerns had been addressed, "we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action"."Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and - most importantly -the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling," he said.The WGA said it continues to believe the deal "will cause damage to writers and the industry at large". The guild said it was forced to settle its own lawsuit because, as a non-profit, it could not afford to fight the merger alone without government support. The studio is set to pay $17.5m into the WGA health fund, cover legal fees, and prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for five years. Bonta said the settlement will help boost film production in the US. Under the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, Bonta said there were strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films. Officials wanted to guarantee "real, robust movies" that generate economic activity and put people back to work, he added. If Paramount fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax. "Divestitures are part of our solutions to all three markets," Bonta said, arguing the deal turned what could have been a "falling off the cliff in domestic production into a huge increase," leading to more movies, jobs, and economic activity. Though Ellison previously indicated the merged company would keep its headquarters in California for the foreseeable future, Bonta clarified that this commitment was not written into the legal agreement. "It's not part of the deal," Bonta said. Ellison had previously threatened to move studio operations out of California. To ensure remaining terms are enforced, Paramount has agreed to the appointment of an independent monitor to oversee ongoing compliance with the settlement. California led the legal push alongside a coalition of state attorneys general from Arizona, Colorado, and New Jersey. Under the deal's initial terms, Paramount must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising over 30% over the following three years. While mergers typically lead to corporate overlap and redundancies, Bonta maintained that it would be a "job creator" that will put people back to work across the industry. Thanks to the deal, Bonta said that economic activity would be "$300m to $1.5bn more, at minimum, for film and TV production right here in our country"."Importantly, that is the baseline. That is the minimum," Bonta said, noting that production commitments could surge by up to 700% if Congress passes a federal film tax credit.

schema.headline: Paramount reaches settlement with states in $110bn Warner Bros merger

title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
description: The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the histori
body: The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible. "In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux. The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London. Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum.

schema.headline: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry

title: Driver charged over fatal A61 Barnsley crash that killed six people
description: A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving over a crash that killed six people, including two children.Shannen Morgan and Shane Ro
body: A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving over a crash that killed six people, including two children.Shannen Morgan and Shane Roller died along with two of their daughters, nine-year-old Rubie, and Lillie, four, when the family's car collided with a motorbike on the A61 between Barnsley and Wakefield on 21 July 2024.Husband and wife Christopher and Janine Barton, from Barnsley, who were both travelling on the motorcycle, also died in the crash.Christopher Cockell, 50, is due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court in October charged with six counts of causing death by dangerous driving.An inquest previously heard that the silver Ford Focus being driven by Mr Roller, 33, collided head on with the BMW motorcycle being driven by Mr Barton, 56, at about 15:50 BST between Staincross and Newmillerdam.Wakefield Coroner's Court heard the collision happened as the motorcycle was overtaking another vehicle on the single-carriageway road, which had a 50mph (80 km/h) speed limit.Coroner's support officer Phil Marr told the hearing: "As a result of a head-on impact, the car was spun to the side of the road, where it caught fire. "It was not possible to release any of the occupants and all four were pronounced dead by paramedics at the scene."Marr said a pathologist concluded Mr Barton's provisional cause of death was due to head and chest injuries.He said Mrs Barton was "thrown onto the adjacent golf course" in the collision, with her death due to chest injuries.Ms Morgan and van driver Mr Roller, who lived in Athersley, Barnsley, had another daughter, aged 11, who was not with them at the time of the crash.An online fundraising page, set up by a family friend in the wake of the tragedy, raised more than £400,000 for her.In a social media post at the time, Mr Roller's father, Graham, paid tribute to the couple, who he described as an "amazing" mum and dad."Shane wasn't just a son but an amazing father and he had a heart of gold," he wrote."Shannen, our daughter-in-law, was funny and was also an amazing mum and they thought the world of their little family."Co-head teachers of Athersley North Primary School, which Rubie and Lillie had attended, said the girls had been "a delight to teach".In a statement, Clare Storr and Kirsty Wordsworth, said: "The girls were a credit to their parents, who were always incredibly supportive and who will also be greatly missed."Mr and Mrs Barton, 48, who had lived in Barnsley, had recently celebrated their 25th wedding anniversary.In a tribute issued via West Yorkshire Police in 2024, their son described his parents as "a loving, caring mum and dad who always put me before everything else".A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said Cockell had been summoned following an investigation by the force's Major Collision Enquiry Team and would appear before magistrates on 28 October.Cockell, of Gresford Close, Woolley Grange, had already been facing a charge of failing to stop at the scene of a collision.

schema.headline: Driver charged over fatal A61 Barnsley crash that killed six people

title: BBC removes 11 Mitchell and Webb comedy sketches from iPlayer
description: The BBC has removed nearly a dozen comedy sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after deciding they no longer "work today".The Bafta-winning comed
body: The BBC has removed nearly a dozen comedy sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after deciding they no longer "work today".The Bafta-winning comedy, written by and starring David Mitchell and Robert Webb, originally ran for four series between 2006 and 2010.The show recently returned to the BBC's iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary. But 11 old sketches, including one that reportedly showed the comedy duo satirising racism while in blackface, have now been cut.A BBC spokesman said in a statement: "This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don't."The Times reported, external the removed material included scenes featuring the English comic actors as war re-enactors in blackface, a sketch about a contestant on a makeover show wearing a burka and a "tribe" living in a garden centre.BBC News has asked Mitchell and Webb - who rose to prominence on the popular Channel 4 sitcom Peep Show - for a comment.That Mitchell and Webb Look grew out of a similar radio show titled That Mitchell and Webb Sound, which began on Radio 4 in 2003, and went on to win the Bafta for best comedy programme in 2007.Defending the double act, fellow comedian Dom Joly, of Trigger Happy TV, questioned the BBC's "censorship" of itself.Joly told The Times: "I totally get it if the BBC is putting out something really racist, which is laughing at and encouraging other people to feel that it's OK to do that."But it's so clear that Mitchell and Webb are not doing that. Their intent was not to be racist."Jimmy Mulville, the co-founder of Hat Trick Productions, which makes the satirical news quiz Have I Got News For You, told the same newspaper he could understand the corporation's predicament."The BBC are in an impossible position," he said.He added that producers had "to be careful", though, "that this is not the thin end of a wedge where we cut things out".Perhaps Mitchell and Webb's best known sketch, which sees them both dressed as Nazis while begging the question: "are we the baddies?", remains online.They are not the first comedians to have had their work edited or removed in recent years, as societal attitudes have shifted. Some artists themselves also began reassessing their work in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement.Matt Lucas and David Walliams' hit show Little Britain was removed from iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox in 2020, after objections resurfaced about some of their characters portraying people from different ethnic backgrounds.At the time, both the BBC and Britbox noted how "times have changed" since the Little Britain first aired in the early noughties.The show is now back on iPlayer but, like with Mitchell and Webb, some sketches have been removed.

schema.headline: BBC removes 11 Mitchell and Webb comedy sketches from iPlayer

title: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring
description: Image source, McQueenImage caption, Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fus
body: Image source, McQueenImage caption, Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fused severe tailoring with dark romanticismByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporter and Emma LynchPicture EditorThis London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs. The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years  of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us".Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses.Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers.Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth".Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026:Messy girl aestheticImage source, Shutterstock/Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Rejecting "quiet luxury" uniforms, Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey, and Conner Ives led London Fashion Week's embrace of the "messy girl" aesthetic by championing deliberate chaos, pairing intentionally undone tailoring and messy updos"The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season.She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year.Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion. She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy".This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives.Gardening-coreImage source, NOWFASHION via Shutterstock/Getty Images/Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Erdem, Yuhan Wang, and Bora Aksu channelled a "gardencore" vibe, trading quiet luxury for unpolished, allotment-ready chaos - pairing parkas and structured trench outerwear with kitchen-garden detailsAccording to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world.A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower. "There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats. It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu.Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show.Modern goddessImage source, Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Dujancourt's free-spirited aesthetic, organic draping, trailing ribbons, and delicately hitched slip skirtsWhilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film. Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer.Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes".Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics.Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide."Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes.OrangeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi showcased some orange Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year.Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet's matching neon outfits , externalat the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway.Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days.BalletImage source, Victor VIRGILE/Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, A school sports hall is transformed into a ballet stage for Edeline Lee's latest collection which drew inspiration from the intense discipline, repetition, and physical toll of classical danceEver the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet.After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year.Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall. "Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel."Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

schema.headline: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring

title: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 09:49 BSTIt may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 09:49 BSTIt may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working?The current state pension is soon likely to top £13,000 a year.Yet one in eight people surveyed by the UK tax authority have never checked how much money they are forecast to receive.Here's how to find out, and what you can do now to boost it.How much is the state pension?If you're working, it is highly likely you're contributing to the state pension - paid by the government when you hit pension age in your late 60s. At the moment:the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week (£12,547.60 a year)the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week (£9,614.80 a year)Many people on the old basic state pension may receive a top-up called the additional state pension. How do I qualify for it?Workers pay National Insurance (NI) contributions. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension.You may have gaps in your NI record if, for example, you have lived abroad. If you've taken time away from work to care for children or family members, then you get NI credits if you receive child benefit or carer's allowance.It's possible to boost your contribution history with voluntary payments. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years.That's one reason why it is important to check your state pension forecast well before you retire, experts say.How do I check what I'll get?You can see what you are forecast to receive:By downloading the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) app, externalUsing the official online state pension forecast webpage, externalTo get a state pension, you will need to prove your identity using official photo ID.Importantly, never click on a link sent in an unsolicited email or text message, even if it looks official, as it could be a scam.For more general information about tax and pensions, HMRC has launched a Tax Confident website, external.And the government-funded, independent Money Helper website has a free retirement guidance tool, external to walk you through the options.Why haven't you checked?The most common reason for not checking a state pension forecast was feeling that retirement was still too far away to think about, a recent survey of 5,000 consumers by HMRC found.Losing track of pension pots from previous jobs, and concerns about how career breaks might affect their entitlement, were also frequent responses.People aged 45-54 were the most likely to have never checked."Whether retirement is decades away or just around the corner, I'd encourage everyone to check their forecast and see if there's anything they can do now to boost their entitlement later," says Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer.

schema.headline: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check

title: Andy Burnham says UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' support
description: Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, in response to attacks the country has faced fro
body: Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, in response to attacks the country has faced from the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.It is understood this is likely to begin in the coming days and will involve a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.The prime minister said it follows a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.Government officials said the offer is "time limited" and likely, in the first instance, to last "for weeks".The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.In recent days, the Houthis in Yemen say they have carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.Defensive support is described by UK officials as that which aides Saudi air force jets shooting down incoming Houthi missiles and drones.The singular Voyager aircraft is part of a core fleet of nine - eight military registered and another civilian registered - on the Royal Air Force (RAF)'s books.The RAF also has five others available for military recall if needed.Speaking to reporters travelling with him on the way to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Burnham linked cost of living pressures to the decision."I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region," he said."Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request."Shipping routes through the Red Sea are a vital artery of the world economy.The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to the Red Sea - a key shipping route used by Saudi Arabia.In a BBC interview last week, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte hinted that European support for Saudi Arabia was likely.He said: "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'."Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful."Energy Minister Martin McCluskey last week told MPs that the UK was "providing air defence support" to Saudi Arabia through the defence partnership that they have, although would not be drawn on questions of operational military activity.In January 2024, the UK joined the US in launching air strikes against Houthi targets across Yemen.Then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the UK "acted in self-defence" following the Houthis' targeting of ships, including a Royal Navy warship.He also said the strikes were "necessary, proportionate, and targeted" to protect lives and commercial shipping.Further joint air strikes from the UK and US followed in 2024, external.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham says UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' support

title: Friedrich Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeatsByKatya AdlerEur
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeatsByKatya AdlerEurope editorGermany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker.The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them.The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield.At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began. German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems.He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks. The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament.Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well. It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist.The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The AfD, led by Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel, has surged in national opinion pollsThe party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want.Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party.The AfD accuses Merz of  failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets.High time for political change, says the AfD.Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician. Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party.I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual. Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted.Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed.He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required.Figure caption, Why Merz is staying on as German chancellor after election 'disaster'But German patience is running thin.Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future.Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped. Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people.Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology. In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive".Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect.Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, As the AfD squeezes the CDU on the right, the left wing Die Linke party attracts voters elsewhere Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget.When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable.Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example.This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech.Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels.The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern.These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls.Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

schema.headline: Friedrich Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability

title: Will Earl Spencer's Diana book damage the monarchy?

body: The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should we believe the unusually robust denial from Buckingham Palace?But when you read further through the book, there's a more complicated story being told.Earl Spencer is the brother watching events unfolding in the strange and ultimately doomed life of his sister, who has stepped from being his childhood companion to become one of the most famous women in the world.He describes a kind of grief and irritation as Diana becomes public property and then royal property, which irks him even more, disliking the "nonsense of fawning" around the monarchy.It's a stark reminder that Diana was only just 20 years old when she married - becoming a global superstar - and was dead 16 years later.Earl Spencer depicts her as a caring, generous character who was haunted by self-doubt, dogged by eating disorders, lacking in warmth from her new royal family and then ultimately dragged down by the tabloid media."She craved acceptance, admiration, kindness, and - perhaps above all - love," writes Charles Spencer about Diana."She got stuck into gritty, controversial, but crucial causes partly because she had a fine, natural social conscience, but also to assuage nagging feelings of worthlessness."And with a memoir like this it will be the extra details that will fascinate people.The stepmother to Diana and Charles, Raine Spencer, is painted in an unflattering light, and Diana is described as getting so angry once that she pushed Raine down the staircase at their home in Althorp. "Raine fortunately landed flush on her buttocks, rather than on bone, and got up, leaving the saloon without a backwards glance," he writes. It was in response, says the book, to Raine telling Diana: "I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you."There's not a single mention of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, even though she was talked about in the TV interviewsWe're told that a "nephew" wanted Earl Spencer to be in a documentary about Diana, which will raise speculation about Prince Harry's plans for his mother's 30th anniversary next yearThe book recounts that she disliked Dodi Fayed's father, Mohammed Fayed, accusing him of crudely groping herDiana's preferences included the soap opera Crossroads and the music of David Bowie. She'd watched The Sound of Music 16 times and the paper she read was the Daily MailEarl Spencer will ultimately be remembered by the passionate eulogy he delivered at Diana's funeral in Westminster Abbey.He reveals how he had pretended to have lost his copy of his speech at the rehearsal, so no one could hear it in advance and try to tone down his stinging criticism of the press and the royals.After the hounding of Diana by the paparazzi, he says he personally rang tabloid newspaper editors to disinvite them from the Abbey funeral, after their invitations had already been sent out.She was buried on an island in the Spencers' Althorp estate, rather than a graveyard - and the book describes how a bishop was brought to consecrate the ground to make it possible.Much of the interest in this book has been driven by its settling of old scores with the Royal Family. It can feel like medieval barons jousting.References to King Charles are almost all negative, including the suggestion that he was jealous of his wife's public popularity.The book reports a conversation in which it's claimed the then-Prince Charles complained: "I mean, I'm 43,' he said, 'and I employ fifty people' – he was flushed in the face now – 'but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!'"The King is portrayed as resentful, with a "senior courtier" reporting an alleged comment by the late Queen: "He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet."There's a bizarre account of discussions in the Royal Family about whether the then-Prince Charles's ears should have been pinned back.And there's the allegation that Diana had said the King was in love with his valet, which the author himself says seemed improbable.What comes across is how close the Spencers were to the royals - but without being friends. Charles and Diana Spencer went to the same children's parties as the young royals.The royals are depicted as the type of children who come round, break your toys and then disappear, in what might be an extended metaphor for how he saw Diana's story.There's also a story about a teenage Prince Andrew smirking in a church service because the priest used the word "womb".While the TV interviews have sought Spencer's views on Prince Harry and Prince William, the book doesn't go there.Earl Spencer describes his opposition to the boys having to walk behind the coffin at their mother's funeral - and he talks of "how tiny, and slight, and bereft, Harry looked".But the focus of this book is much more about the Diana era - and an elegy to the lost world of their childhood.Earl Spencer emphasises its country house happiness, with dens, dogs and horses, but it's also dotted with cruelty, with violent nannies and the "mindless and often destructive" tradition of boarding schools.A boy who accidentally shot and killed his father gets the mawkish nickname "Baghdad".Although the book is about Diana, it's also about its author, the younger brother trying to make sense of what's happened - and also, like many younger brothers, being able to criticise without being able to take responsibility.Earl Spencer talks about how little he cares for "archaic" titles for the aristocracy or royals.And in this book, the title that seems really to have shaped his life most is "Diana's brother".Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, by Charles Spencer. Published by Penguin.

schema.headline: Will Earl Spencer's Diana book damage the monarchy?

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
description: Trump later reacted to news of the lawsuit, calling the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and de
body: Trump later reacted to news of the lawsuit, calling the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements. "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.He added that "almost without question" his team will file an appeal.The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.The statement from CNN, Politico and MS NOW said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting."Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."The media organisations filed the lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington, asking a judge to quickly rule Trump's ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it.On Monday morning, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties, which sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place".CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally due to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday.But on Monday morning, the five-seat CNN booth in the basement of the White House press area - typically manned throughout the day from the early hours of the morning - was empty and closed. Screens and monitors inside were turned off.Instead, a CNN crew was outside the secured area of the White House grounds, broadcasting live from a public pavement.Five TV networks, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, issued a joint statement: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government."No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."Those five networks are considered the only ones with the money and infrastructure to distribute live coverage from the White House and presidential events.For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York, where he will meet Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday.Announcing his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".The US president added that there "may be others to join them".When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. But unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS Now and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

schema.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president open to reform and external review of football's governing body
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform.In a le
body: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform.In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino explains the independent process would "recommend potential improvements".Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened".This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives".Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash.In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you", and says the consultation will be with confederations, member associations and "relevant stakeholders".He insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!"His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not."Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be."He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together".Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves.FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football."We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association," he adds in the letter."What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided."The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead."Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan.The 56-year-old Swiss-Italian Fifa leader will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents.Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.Having defiantly clung to power for weeks amid an unprecedented rebellion over his presidency, this is a significant change in tone from Infantino - and the first sign that he may feel he has no choice but to compromise if he is to win another re-election in March.On 15 October, the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since this crisis began, and Infantino will no doubt hope that this relieves some of the pressure he is under.But even if he is prepared to accept some changes to the way Fifa is run, will that be enough to win over some of those that have turned against him?As well as wanting him to step down, many of Infantino's critics want an overhaul of Fifa's governance, with curbs on the president's power (such as a maximum of a single term in office), more separation between the president and the Fifa administration, greater emphasis on human rights and sustainability, and the redistribution of Fifa's cash reserves.It will be fascinating to see if Infantino is prepared to accept such changes if it means staying in power.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president open to reform and external review of football's governing body

title: Bishop of Lincoln resigns amid sexual assault inquiry
description: The Bishop of Lincoln, the Right Reverend Stephen Conway, has resigned amid an ongoing investigation into an allegation of sexual assault.It follows h
body: The Bishop of Lincoln, the Right Reverend Stephen Conway, has resigned amid an ongoing investigation into an allegation of sexual assault.It follows his arrest in February.Conway's resignation, which will formally come into effect on 1 October, was confirmed in a statement from the Church of England."The complaint process is ongoing. Clergy remain subject to church disciplinary procedures following resignation or retirement," it said.Conway had been suspended from ministry in February when a "safeguarding complaint" was made.At the time, Lincolnshire Police said the arrest was part of an "ongoing investigation following an allegation that a man was sexually assaulted between 2018 and 2025".Following Conway's resignation, the Church said Dr Nicholas Chamberlain, the Bishop of Grantham, would continue as Acting Bishop of Lincoln until a permanent replacement is chosen.Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

schema.headline: Bishop of Lincoln resigns amid sexual assault inquiry

title: Gary Neville: Was Manchester United legend right to call out former club for 'lac of effort'?
description: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic."Gary Neville did not hold b
body: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic."Gary Neville did not hold back in his criticism of Manchester United's performance during Sky Sports' coverage of Sunday's 1-1 draw at Fulham.The players had just laboured through the opening stages of the second half, culminating in a Lisandro Martinez own goal gifting the home side the lead."I've never seen such a lack of effort," Neville added. "What must Michael Carrick be thinking?"Neville played 602 games for United over a 19-year career, winning everything the club game had to offer. So his criticism comes from a qualified position.This season's out-of-possession stats would appear to back it up too, with the Red Devils ranking 16th for distance covered, and 17th for total number of sprints.But does that tell the whole story?How did United play under Carrick when they were winning games towards the end of last season?And, as Neville makes the headlines, what does this say about his influence in the media around Manchester United?United's dismal running and sprinting stats made for stark reading in the wake of Neville's criticism.After all, the former right-back had directly questioned a lack of effort, and referred to the players as "mannequins".He said United - and Fulham - were walking too much during the game.In the Premier League this season only four teams have covered less distance than the Red Devils, and just three teams have produced fewer sprints.It comes alongside United's joint-worst start to a Premier League season, with four points from five games.So is this down to the running and the effort?Let's take a look at the second half of last season, after Carrick had been appointed as manager.Between 17 January and the end of the season, United picked up more points than any other team - 39 points from 17 games.Yet only four teams ran less than United, and only two clubs had fewer sprints.There is no material difference in the running stats, but United were returning 2.29 points per game compared to the 0.8 this season.Something is clearly different, but it does not appear to be linked to this particular stat because barely anything has changed - apart from the results. Maybe this United squad simply does not have runners.Then there is the comparison to rival teams.Manchester City have won all five Premier League matches but have covered less distance than United. Enzo Maresca's squad have also recorded the lowest number of sprints in the division.Brighton, one of the most exciting teams in the league this season and the top goalscorers, are one place above United for sprints.Maybe United's problem is tactical rather than a simple case of not running enough?Neville setting the media agenda when it comes to United is not a new thing.The former England international has called out the team's shortcomings on many occasions.Look back to December 2021, and a poor first-half performance against a struggling Newcastle side when Ralf Rangnick's side trailed 1-0 at the break."They're a bunch of whinge-bags," Neville said at half-time on Sky Sports. "I'll not go into names but they're whinging at each other, arms up in the air complaining about everything."There's no pressing, no urgency, the basics of the game."Edinson Cavani rescued a point at St James' Park, but Neville's comments had already made the headlines.You only need to look at how the post-match coverage went after the Fulham draw.Neville's remarks were put to Carrick at full-time. The United manager said fitness levels of his players were not an issue.But the die was cast."Neville: That was the worst ever", read the back page of Monday's Daily Telegraph."15 minutes of shame", was the lead for the sports section of the Daily Star."United boss keeps calm after Neville Ful blast," said the Daily Express.It was picked up across online media, and discussed at length on radio talk shows - including across the BBC, as evidenced by this piece.When Neville criticises his former club, it carries weight.In January, with Ruben Amorim under pressure for poor results, the Portuguese head coach said that "if people cannot handle the Gary Nevilles and the criticisms of everything, we need to change the club".Amorim was dismissed the following day.There always seems to be a strong influence in the media related to the dominant team of a previous era.For example, throughout the 1990s and 2000s, former Liverpool stars such as Alan Hansen, Mark Lawrenson and Phil Thompson dominated a lot of the conversation.It stands to reason that now members of the all-conquering United squad will have a leading role in the media.But for Neville, it is bigger than anyone apart from Gary Lineker and his Goalhanger production company."When does Sky wonder if they are paying a lot of money in wages to train their next competitor?"It is a question posed by Richard Gillis, who hosts the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast.While Neville started out in the media as a pundit with Sky Sports, the 51-year-old is now one of the biggest players in a rapidly changing industry.After co-founding the sports entertainment production company Buzz16 in 2016, Neville launched YouTube platform The Overlap in 2021.The Overlap produces Stick to Football - one of the UK's most popular football content channels with 2.2 billion views across all platforms in 2025.Earlier this year it entered into a strategic partnership with radio giants Global, with the aim to create a multi-format sports media network.Neville this summer exited Buzz16, focusing his attention on The Overlap, which has branched out into cricket and rugby, and secured live Bundesliga rights.The YouTube channels of United influencer Mark Goldbridge were recently acquired, a further sign of the influence Neville now wields in football's media industry.Goldbridge made his name with expletive-laden rants during streamed 'watchalongs' of United matches, and his channels have about four million subscribers.Gillis points out that Neville was attracted to the Goldbridge brand, and his United Stand podcast, because it creates noise when there is no football."Noise is valuable," Gillis told BBC Sport. "Man Utd generate more of it than any other club in the Premier League."Anger creates engagement. And from the Sky commentary box, Neville is well placed to create anger."In a bid to ramp up its content, The Overlap is believed to have targeted national newspaper journalists to come on board and cover United."It poses questions," Gillis says of this development."Currently, Neville is the story. He says something, the media reports it, the fans respond to it. A valuable loop."At what point does The Overlap and the United Stand [a Goldbridge channel] become the rivals of the media?"What is the United Stand now? A noise merchant, or a news organisation?"To many, it probably does not matter whether Neville's comments about United's running are valid or not.They create headlines, column inches and legitimate talking points under the Sky Sports name.Yet Neville is himself a media mogul who also works within another organisation.And at present, when measured by media coverage and impact, all parties are winners.

schema.headline: Gary Neville: Was Manchester United legend right to call out former club for 'lac of effort'?
